content: Periodic surveys can provide critical information similar to that obtained from continuous surveillance systems. However, they are limited in their ability to detect localized outbreaks, may yield results with margins of error that hinder meaningful analysis or trend determination, and are subject to biases inherent in sampling methods. Despite these limitations, surveys can offer secondary benefits, such as strengthening laboratory capacity, improving transport and referral systems, and evaluating the accuracy of patient classification based on treatment history. Nationwide surveys are ideal for programmatic purposes, but in large countries with insufficient national capacity or specific concerns, such as a suspected increase in drug-resistant tuberculosis (TB) in certain regions, surveys at subnational administrative levels may also be considered. The size and scope of a survey should align with its specific objectives and the ability of the National Tuberculosis Program (NTP) to ensure quality. Starting with surveys at lower administrative levels, such as cities or provinces, before expanding to nationwide surveys, can help build capacity while maintaining quality. However, results from subnational surveys cannot be extrapolated to estimate the national burden. In settings lacking the capacity for continuous surveillance based on routine drug susceptibility testing (DST) of new TB cases, surveys should be conducted at least every five years. These surveys provide critical information on the burden of resistance and common drug resistance profiles among patients at a specific point in time. Sentinel surveillance systems may be an option for monitoring trends in drug resistance over time in countries with limited resources, healthcare infrastructure, or geographical challenges that preclude routine DST for all patients. Sentinel systems can serve as an interim approach for countries aiming to expand routine DST to all cases. However, such systems require careful planning to produce useful data and have limitations, including the inability to provide nationwide data or infer trends for the entire country. Sentinel systems are recommended only for countries with high-quality data from a recent survey (within the past five years) and those transitioning toward establishing a national routine surveillance system. The classification of patient treatment history is critical for accurate interpretation of surveillance data. According to the 2013 WHO framework, a new case refers to a newly registered episode of TB in a patient who has never been treated for TB or has taken anti-TB drugs for less than one month. A previously treated case refers to a newly registered episode of TB in a patient who has received one month or more of anti-TB drugs in the past. Previously treated cases, also known as retreatment cases, are a heterogeneous group that includes subcategories such as relapse patients, treatment after failure, treatment after loss to follow-up, and others with unknown or undocumented outcomes from their most recent treatment. Evaluating resistance among subcategories of previously treated cases is essential for data interpretation and program management. These patients are at higher risk of harboring drug-resistant TB strains and are often screened for inclusion in drug-resistant TB treatment programs. Information on the size, composition, and resistance patterns of this population is crucial for programmatic planning and can be collected through routine culture and DST of all such cases. Stratifying drug resistance data by age groups, sex, HIV status, and other patient characteristics can provide insights into risk groups and the effectiveness of TB control activities. For example, drug resistance among younger age groups is more likely to reflect recent transmission, while older age groups may harbor older infections. Incorporating HIV testing into drug resistance surveillance can yield valuable information on the relationship between HIV and drug-resistant TB. Provider-initiated HIV testing is recommended for all TB patients and those presenting with TB symptoms. National policies on HIV testing and surveillance, including counseling, consent, and confidentiality, should be followed. The national HIV/AIDS program should be involved in planning and executing surveillance activities. Surveys can also serve as a platform for studying setting-specific causes of drug resistance and identifying key targets for intervention. They may include questions about potential risk factors, such as antiretroviral treatment in HIV-positive patients, socioeconomic status, education level, malnutrition, crowding, diabetes, alcohol abuse, drug use, or smoking. For previously treated patients, additional information on the type and quality of previous treatment, infection control practices, and drug sources may be collected. Multiple risk factors for the acquisition, amplification, and transmission of drug resistance may coexist in a given setting. Quality-assured laboratory methods are essential for reliable drug resistance surveillance. The introduction of rapid diagnostic methods for identifying Mycobacterium tuberculosis and performing DST should be prioritized. Recent technological advances have expanded WHO-recommended methods for DST, significantly reducing the time between TB detection and drug resistance diagnosis. Rapid DST methods enable timely selection of appropriate treatment regimens and increase surveillance capacity. WHO has endorsed nucleic acid amplification tests (NAATs), such as Xpert MTB/RIF, which provide results in approximately 90 minutes and detect rifampicin resistance. However, additional DST methods may be needed to investigate resistance to other drugs. Molecular line probe assays (LPAs) are genotypic DST methods endorsed by WHO for detecting rifampicin and isoniazid resistance in smear-positive sputum samples or M. tuberculosis cultures. While useful for surveillance, LPAs are less sensitive for detecting isoniazid resistance and may underestimate resistance levels. Phenotypic DST methods using liquid or solid culture media remain common. Liquid culture methods are faster and more sensitive than solid media but require specific infrastructure and biosafety measures. Solid culture methods, while inexpensive and standardized, take longer to produce results. The proportion method is the most widely used solid culture technique globally.
